public_rationale: Ramp repeats a previous finding that 1% of sampled firms account for 80% of observed spending on OpenAI and Anthropic [e1]. It does not identify those firms' products or subscription terms [e1]. An October 25, 2026 secondary account reports venture backing among top AI spenders, but distinguishes that group from the OpenAI-and-Anthropic spending cohort [e2]. It does not establish that the groups contain the same firms [e2]. Neither source settles whether a vast majority of the referenced cohort are AI product startups predominantly offering monthly plans that permit token costs far above subscription receipts [e1] [e2].
limitations: Ramp's sampled spending is not a measure of the providers' total revenue, and the repeated 80% statistic has no explicit observation period in the passage [e1].
Venture backing does not establish the claimed products or subscription arrangements [e2].
The evidence does not link the September 2026 cohort to subscription allowances and actual token procurement costs [e1] [e2].

public_payload.normalized_proposition: From what he hears, the vast majority of the 1% of customers behind most OpenAI and Anthropic revenue are AI startups that power their products with those models, predominantly through monthly subscriptions that let users burn far more in tokens than the subscriptions earn.

statement.excerpt: From what I hear, the vast majority of those 1% of customers are AI startups that power their products using OpenAI and Anthropic’s models, predominantly using monthly subscriptions that allow users to burn way more in tokens than their subscriptions actually make.

from_speaker: the vast majority of those 1% of customers
power their products using OpenAI and Anthropic’s models
allow users to burn way more in tokens than their subscriptions actually make
our_interpretation: Treat 'from what I hear' as attribution to unnamed sources, not a conditional forecast.
Read 'those 1%' as the high-spending customer group referenced in the Ramp chart. Do not silently equate Ramp's sample with the providers' entire customer bases.
Vast majority means a large majority by customer count; no precise percentage is supplied.
The subscription statement concerns permitted usage, not proof that the average subscriber exhausts the allowance.
Use September 2026, the latest complete month before the post, for the ongoing customer-composition claim.
The principal test is customer composition and business-model prevalence, not a numerical revenue estimate.
criteria.support_condition: A representative breakdown of the referenced top-spending cohort shows a large majority are AI product startups using these models, and that monthly plans permitting substantially greater token expense than subscription receipts predominate among them.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable customer-level evidence shows the cohort is not largely composed of those startups, or that the described subscription arrangements do not predominate.

evidence.explanation: Confirms the concentration premise in Ramp's observed spending. It does not identify those firms or establish their subscription terms, so it cannot settle the proposition.

evidence.excerpt: Third, being venture-backed doesn't mean the bills are paid with venture money.
evidence.locator: Paragraph summarizing Tunguz's three methodological limits
evidence.explanation: The later discussion offers potentially relevant evidence about venture backing, but that classification does not establish token resale, subsidized subscriptions or the source of payments. Its discussion also distinguishes the two top-spender rankings.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A representative September 2026 breakdown of the exact referenced cohort, with its ranking method and customer classifications, linked to model use, monthly subscription terms, maximum permitted usage and actual token procurement costs. This would test both the claimed startup majority and the prevalence of the described plans.
